record.original_question: Among all planar graphs on n >= 9 vertices, is the graph K_2 joined with the path P_{n-2} always the one with maximum spectral radius?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 5 (Boots-Royle 1991 [25] and independently Cao-Vince 1993 [32]). Among all planar graph on n ≥ 9 vertices, K2 ∨ Pn−2 attains the maximum spectral radius.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G be a simple finite graph. The spectral radius of G is the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix. A graph is planar if it can be embedded in the plane without edge crossings. For two vertex-disjoint graphs H_1 and H_2, the join H_1 ∨ H_2 is obtained from the disjoint union of H_1 and H_2 by adding all edges between V(H_1) and V(H_2). Let K_2 denote the complete graph on 2 vertices and P_{n-2} denote the path on n-2 vertices.

Prove or disprove: for every integer n ≥ 9, among all planar graphs on n vertices, the graph K_2 ∨ P_{n-2} attains the maximum spectral radius.
artifact.category_tag: Spectral graph theory / planar extremal graphs
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture was proved by Tait and Tobin for all sufficiently large n, but the full statement for every n ≥ 9 remains unresolved. Subsequent work (e.g., a 2025 preprint) extends the result to additional ranges of n (such as n ≥ 48 under restriction to planar graphs with a dominating vertex), but no source confirms a complete resolution for all n ≥ 9.

status_evidence.title: Three conjectures in extremal spectral graph theory (Tait–Tobin)
status_evidence.snippet: Tait and Tobin proved that K_2 ∨ P_{n-2} attains the maximum spectral radius among planar graphs for sufficiently large n.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is proved for sufficiently large n.

status_evidence.title: On the maximum spectral radius of planar graphs (2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Among all planar graphs containing a dominating vertex with fixed order n ≥ 48, the join of P_2 and P_{n-2} attains the maximum spectral radius; the conjecture for concrete fixed order is still open.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture for concrete fixed order remains open in general.
